newsitem.title: TURKEY: Hopes fade for Turkey scandal outcome.
newsitem.headline: Hopes fade for Turkey scandal outcome.

text.p: Hopes have faded that Turkish officials will ever uncover the full extent of murky ties among right-wing mobsters, drug dealers and elements of the political and security establishment, commentators said on Tuesday.

Parliamentary and judicial probes into a security scandal have been limited despite months of press accusations that high-ranking officials encouraged anti-rebel death squads run by gangsters and crack policemen.
"It has turned out to be a damp squib," investigative journalist Ismet Berkan of the Radikal daily told Reuters.
A senior policeman and a gangster wanted for murder both died in a crash at the town of Susurluk last November, setting off a campaign against so-called state gangs.
Government MP Sedat Bucak, who heads a tribal militia fighting separatist Kurdish guerrillas, was also in the vehicle. Guns and silencers were found in the wreckage.
The subsequent resignation of interior minister Mehmet Agar and an unprecedented public outcry raised the possibility of a thorough inquiry into alleged official links to organised crime.

The media and opposition called for a revision of the fight against Kurdish rebels in the southeast because of the number of area policemen, soldiers and repentant guerrillas said to be involved in drug smuggling and common crime.

Only 10 people, most of them low-ranking policemen, however have been charged by an Istanbul court investigating the crash. A court in the southeastern town of Yuksekova has arrested other security forces members in a similar case.
"A few people who have already confessed will take the rap for this and political personalities will not be called to account," said Berkan.
Attempts to lift the parliamentary immunity of Bucak and Agar have been caught up in red tape that government critics say is a deliberate attempt to cover up the affair.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's office has spent more than a month deciding whether to ask parliament if the MPs, from his True Path Party coalition partners, should be tried.
A parliamentary commission looking into the scandal split along party lines this month in a row whether to question True Path leader and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller and a top general.
Coalition MPs later voted to halt the probe.
"It was government intervention," said commission member Yasar Topcu, from the main opposition Motherland Party.
"There were still contradictions between witnesses' statements to be sorted out. There were a lot of people still to be spoken to," he said.
The inquiry is to announce its findings next week but parliament does not have to act on any of its recommendations.
The scandal stirred public reaction despite the lack of official action. Protesters took to the streets every night in the month of February in candlelit marches to call for clean government.

"Susurluk can be hidden temporarily for the moment but it cannot be covered up completely. Perhaps the next government will be under a lot of pressure if it becomes an election issue at some time in the future," Berkan said.
